title: Trump Extends $100K H-1B Fee to 2027 Even as Courts Block Collection
excerpt: The Sept. 18 extension keeps the $100,000 H-1B payment alive through Sept. 2027 — but two federal judges have barred agencies from collecting it while the administration's appeal plays out.
body:
• President Donald Trump signed Proclamation 11069 on Sept. 18, 2026, extending the $100,000 payment requirement for certain new H-1B petitions through Sept. 21, 2027. The fee is not currently being collected.
  • A Massachusetts judge vacated the fee in June, ruling it an unconstitutional tax the executive branch had no authority to impose; the First Circuit refused to pause that ruling in July. A second federal judge in California on Sept. 30 blocked immigration agencies from implementing the fee — including the new extension — while litigation continues.
  • The payment applies only to new, consular-processed H-1B petitions for workers hired from outside the U.S. Extensions, renewals, change-of-employer petitions, and F-1 students changing status inside the U.S. are exempt — but some immigration attorneys say USCIS is sitting on affected petitions without adjudicating them.
  • Separately, the Department of Homeland Security has proposed a permanent ~$103,265 fee for many cap-subject H-1B petitions through formal rulemaking. If both stood, employers could face more than $200,000 in additional fees per overseas hire.

A fee on the books, but no one is paying it

President Donald Trump extended his administration's $100,000 H-1B visa fee on Sept. 18, keeping the controversial policy alive on paper through Sept. 21, 2027 — even as federal courts have repeatedly barred it from being enforced. Proclamation 11069, which reached the Federal Register on Sept. 23, extends the original September 2025 proclamation that imposed a $100,000 payment on many new H-1B petitions for workers hired from outside the United States.

The extension changes little on the ground. The fee has been unenforceable since late July, and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has not assessed the payment since.

Two courts, two legal paths, same result

The first blow came in June 2026, when U.S. District Judge Leo T. Sorokin of the District of Massachusetts struck down the policy in a lawsuit brought by 20 states. Sorokin concluded the $100,000 payment "was not a penalty but a tax" — and that Congress, not the president, holds the taxing power. His order vacated the policy in full and barred collection by USCIS and the State Department. When the administration appealed, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit declined on July 24 to pause the ruling, keeping the fee blocked.

The second defeat arrived Sept. 30. U.S. District Judge Haywood S. Gilliam Jr. of the Northern District of California enjoined USCIS, Customs and Border Protection, and the State Department from implementing the fee in Global Nurse Force v. Trump, a case brought by a coalition of employers, labor unions, health care providers, schools, and nonprofits. Gilliam found the agencies had skipped the notice-and-comment rulemaking the Administrative Procedure Act requires before imposing rules of such broad effect — and that the underlying policies were likely arbitrary and capricious. Crucially, his order covers both the original proclamation and the Sept. 18 extension.

Why extend a fee that isn't being collected?

Immigration practitioners read the extension as a legal maneuver rather than an enforcement one. The original proclamation carried a one-year term and would otherwise have lapsed on Sept. 21, 2026. Extending it keeps the framework in place so the fee could take effect quickly if an appeals court rules for the administration — and it signals the White House intends to keep pressing the policy, which employers may factor into hiring plans.

The same week as the extension, Trump also signed an executive order directing agencies to scrutinize employers that have laid off American workers and to review previously filed labor condition applications for enforcement. DHS separately published a proposed rule in August setting a permanent ~$103,265 fee for many cap-subject H-1B petitions; the public comment period drew more than 10,000 comments.

What it means for Indian workers and employers

Indians are by far the largest beneficiaries of the H-1B program, receiving roughly three-quarters of all H-1B visas in recent years, so the stakes for the diaspora are direct. The fee was designed to hit precisely the pathway most Indian tech workers use: new hires applying from outside the United States.

For now, applicants and employers should know that no $100,000 payment is being assessed. But the legal limbo has its own cost — immigration attorneys report that USCIS is sitting on some affected petitions without adjudicating them, leaving workers and employers in uncertainty. A separate challenge led by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce is pending before the D.C. Circuit, and the administration's appeal of the Massachusetts ruling continues.

What's next

The immediate question is whether the appeals courts will restore the fee. Until then, the extension and the court orders coexist: a policy on the books, frozen in court. Employers should watch the DHS rulemaking on the separate $103,265 fee — that proposal went through the formal process the courts said was missing, which makes it a far more durable threat to H-1B hiring budgets.
